concepts.head: interactable_entity(X)

justification.excerpt: the entity that the end user or developer interacts with

rules.why: An interactable entity is explicitly defined as the entity that users and developers interact with, which is the assistant.

borrows.gloss: the assistant role in the conversation
borrows.why_undefined: The document defines assistant but does not formalize it as a logic predicate; it would be instantiated from message roles.

concepts.notes: The definition is explicitly stated and unambiguous. The assistant is the sole entity described as interactable in the context.

concepts.head: interaction_entity(X)

justification.excerpt: end user or developer interacts with

rules.why: The end user is explicitly mentioned as one who interacts with the assistant.

justification.excerpt: end user or developer interacts with

rules.why: The developer is explicitly mentioned as one who interacts with the assistant.

borrows.gloss: a user of a product made by OpenAI or a third-party application
borrows.why_undefined: This is a core entity type defined in the document but not formalized as a logic predicate; would be instantiated from message context.

borrows.gloss: a customer of the OpenAI API
borrows.why_undefined: This is a core entity type defined in the document but not formalized as a logic predicate; would be instantiated from message roles.

concepts.notes: The document explicitly names end users and developers as the entities that interact with the assistant. No other interaction entities are described.

concepts.head: conflicts_with_later_same_authority(I)

rules.asp: conflicts_with_later_same_authority(I1) :- instruction(I1), instruction(I2), same_authority(I1, I2), later_than(I2, I1), (contradicts(I2, I1) | overrides(I2, I1) | makes_irrelevant(I2, I1)).

justification.excerpt: An instruction is *superseded* if an instruction in a later message at the same level either contradicts it, overrides it, or otherwise makes it irrelevant

rules.why: An instruction conflicts with (is superseded by) a later same-authority instruction if that later instruction contradicts, overrides, or makes the earlier one irrelevant.

borrows.gloss: a directive that the assistant may be asked to follow
borrows.why_undefined: The document defines instruction abstractly but does not specify how to identify instances; varies by context (spec, message).

borrows.gloss: two instructions have the same authority level
borrows.why_undefined: Authority levels are defined (root, system, developer, user, guideline) but the predicate to test equivalence is not formalized.

borrows.gloss: one instruction appears later in the message sequence than another
borrows.why_undefined: Message ordering is implicit in the document but not formalized as a predicate.
The document describes contradiction but leaves its formal definition to context.
The document uses 'overrides' as an example but does not define it formally.

borrows.gloss: one instruction renders another no longer applicable
borrows.why_undefined: The document cites this as a reason for supersession but does not formalize the condition.

concepts.notes: The rule captures the logical structure, but the document leaves the three conditions (contradicts, overrides, makes_irrelevant) underspecified. A real implementation would need to define how to detect each.

concepts.head: refusal_style(S)

justification.excerpt: briefly explain why it cannot provide a full answer, and then do its best to provide safe and useful assistance

rules.why: Safe Complete is one of the two refusal styles described: explaining the constraint and then providing what help is permissible.

justification.excerpt: simply refuse to help (e.g. "Sorry, I can't help with [X]")

rules.why: Simple refusal is the other style: a direct, concise refusal without offering alternative assistance.

concepts.notes: Both refusal styles are explicitly named in the document. These are constants (0-arity predicates promoted to 1-arity by convention). The document is clear on the two approaches.

concepts.head: pasted_text(T)

justification.excerpt: the user might paste (without quotes) some text that they haven't read carefully and includes malicious instructions

rules.why: Pasted text is text that a user pastes without reading carefully, potentially containing malicious instructions.

borrows.gloss: a sequence of characters provided in the input
borrows.why_undefined: Content primitives are assumed but not formalized in the document.

borrows.gloss: the user provided text by pasting (not typing or generating)
borrows.why_undefined: The method of input is mentioned but not formalized as a predicate.

borrows.gloss: the user has not reviewed the text carefully
borrows.why_undefined: The document mentions this state but does not define how it is detected or represented.

concepts.notes: The document describes pasted text in context of a specific risk (malicious content), but does not give a formal definition that separates pasted text from other input. The rule captures the key characteristics: pasted, not read carefully.

concepts.head: policy_class(X, C)

justification.excerpt: even if the resulting output would ordinarily be disallowed as restricted or sensitive content

rules.why: Restricted is one of the two policy classes that the transformation exception concerns; content is classified as restricted.

justification.excerpt: even if the resulting output would ordinarily be disallowed as restricted or sensitive content

rules.why: Sensitive is the other policy class affected by the transformation exception; content is classified as sensitive.

borrows.gloss: content that the model is ordinarily prohibited from producing
borrows.why_undefined: The document describes restricted content (e.g., in stay_in_bounds section) but does not define it as a formal predicate.

borrows.gloss: content marked as sensitive per policy
borrows.why_undefined: Sensitive content is referenced but not formally defined in the transformation_exception section.

concepts.notes: The document identifies exactly two policy classes relevant to the transformation exception. The arity is 2 (content and class), and the rule map content to its class, but the underlying predicates (restricted_content, sensitive_content) would need to be defined elsewhere.

concepts.head: new_material(M)

justification.excerpt: should only output material drawn from the user's own input, without adding new disallowed content

rules.why: New material is material that is not drawn from the user's input—i.e., material added by the assistant.

borrows.gloss: content or information in an output
borrows.why_undefined: Material is a general category but is not formalized as a predicate in the document.

borrows.gloss: the material originates from or is directly copied from user-provided content
borrows.why_undefined: The document emphasizes this principle but does not define a formal test for whether material is drawn from user input.

concepts.notes: The document explicitly contrasts material drawn from user input with new material added by the assistant. The rule is a negation: new material is what is not drawn from the user.

concepts.head: task(T)

justification.excerpt: The assistant may be tasked with complex or multi-step goals

rules.why: A task is a complex goal that the assistant is given to pursue.

justification.excerpt: The assistant may be tasked with complex or multi-step goals

rules.why: A task may also be a multi-step goal, which involves sequential decisions.

borrows.gloss: an objective the assistant is asked to accomplish
borrows.why_undefined: Goals are mentioned but not formalized as a predicate.

borrows.gloss: a goal that involves substantial reasoning or coordination
borrows.why_undefined: Complexity is a relative term; the document does not define thresholds.

borrows.gloss: a goal that requires sequential decisions or actions
borrows.why_undefined: Multi-step is described but not formally defined; what constitutes a step is context-dependent.

concepts.notes: The document describes tasks as complex or multi-step goals but does not formally define task(T) in isolation. The rule assumes that either complexity or multi-step nature qualifies a goal as a task, which may be over-inclusive. A more conservative rule would require both conditions, but the document uses 'or' (via the phrase 'complex or multi-step').
